newsitem.title: USA: US Senate Dems say don't rush budget, tax bills.
newsitem.headline: US Senate Dems say don't rush budget, tax bills.

text.p: Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee asked President Clinton Friday not to rush on legislation to balance the budget and cut taxes if Democratic standards are not met.

The Democrats, led by Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, sent a letter to Clinton saying: "If it is not possible by August 1 to produce legislation that Democrats can in good conscience support, then we urge that action be deferred until September."
Republican leaders have said their goal is to complete the legislation by their August recess.
The Democrats said a lower budget deficit this year lifted some of the urgency from needing quick action on the bills.
Moynihan said the deficit could be about $30 billion at the end of fiscal 1997, which ends September 30, leading to balance next year if current trends continued.

"At a time when our economy is outperforming all expectations and the federal budget is nearing balance for the first time in almost three decades, we believe it is incumbent upon the administration and Democrats in Congress to stand firm for our priorities, and to craft this legislation with great care," the Senate Democrats' letter to Clinton said.
Congressional leaders and tax writers have been meeting with White House officials this week trying to reach an agreement on the balanced-budget and tax bills.
So far, most major issues remained unresolved.
Moynihan said that, due to the complexity of the legislation, more time was needed to consider it and there should not be a rush to reach conclusion in the next four or five days.
